In the military domain, the UK has participated actively in initiatives on AI in the military domain, including the Responsible Uses of AI in the Military Domain summits, REAIM, and US-led political declaration on responsible military use of AI and autonomy. We have also welcomed efforts under the Global Digital Compact to close digital divides and enhance international governance on AI for the benefit of humanity. The UK is confident that initiatives like this lay the foundations for discussions in the UN on how to harness AI capabilities in a way that supports international peace and security. And finally, on hate speech. Recognizing the danger, as we have heard today, of online hate speech as a driver of conflict and the risk it poses to human rights, Working with the Office of the Special Adviser on the Prevention of Genocide, we supported the development of a new methodology for monitoring social media to address and counter online hate speech, thereby providing a tool for the UN, for governments, and technology companies to monitor and prevent hate speech and safeguard human rights. Chair, as we look forward, we must ensure that new initiatives complement our existing efforts. We must continue to assess the capabilities opportunities, risks and challenges that AI presents. Cybersecurity must be a core requirement and primary consideration for any AI system, not just in the development phase but throughout the life cycle of the system. And we must remain vigilant on threats, protecting privacy, fairness, reliability and predictability, and guarding against its irresponsible use. Thank you.
I would like to thank the representative of the United Kingdom for his statement. And now I give the floor to the representative of Algeria.

As host of the third African Startup Conference focused on AI, we demonstrated our commitment to developing AI ecosystems that serves our people needs while respecting security imperatives on how initiatives supporting open inclusive and trustworthy AI contribute to International peace and security we believe the African digital compact provides a clear framework this Continental strategy envisions AI as a driver for positive change and socioeconomic transformation while ensuring its responsible use. Law.

Third, invest in targeted capacity building programs to ensure all countries can assess and address AI related security risks. I would like to thank the representative of Algeria for his statement. And now I give the floor to the representative of Guyana.

Chair, Co-Chairs, in addressing the guiding questions, I offer the following points. First, In supporting the maintenance of international peace and security, it is critical to ensure that AI technology is developed and utilized in a safe and ethical manner. These systems can provide opportunities for bridging digital gaps between developed and developing countries and for enhancing knowledge and experiences. However, to ensure responsible use of AI through these systems, transparency, accountability, and human oversight and control must be prioritized. Open AI systems should also be safe, secure, and reliable. Once these elements are incorporated into open AI systems, the risks of misuse can be reduced, creating a more stable and secure global environment. Second, the UN, including the Security Council, has a role in leveraging the responsible use of AI to advance international peace and security. The UN has already begun to address this topic, including through the Global Digital Compact, the establishment of the Secretary-General's high-level advisory body on AI and the ongoing process to establish an independent scientific panel and a global dialogue on AI. Complementary to this, the Security Council, through its peacekeeping missions, can utilize AI systems to ensure the safety and protection of UN staff and peacekeepers. by predicting and preventing conflicts, improving situational awareness, expanding the overall reach of peacekeeping missions, and decreasing response times, especially for missions operating in challenging terrains. In employing AI systems, however, we must be cognizant of and address the potential for misuse of this technology, including any violations of international law and infringements on the sovereignty of any nation. Dear co-chairs, in closing, Guyana underscores the need for a multilateral approach to dealing with the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence. It is important for us to advance discussions on this topic to derive initiatives and policies that will capitalize on opportunities presented by AI while mitigating the risks associated with its misuse. I thank the representative of Guyana for her statement. And now I give the floor to the Deputy Permanent Representative of Slovenia.

Thank you very much, Chair, and thanks to other organizers for organizing this meeting. I wish to, of course, also thank all the three briefers for their excellent presentations. This past few months, have not only seen the unveiling of new AI models and their subsequent impact on the financial markets, but also an increased concern over, among others, their environmental impact due to substantial energy consumption and related freshwater usage. AI continues to be weaponized and used in contemporary conflicts, putting civilians at an even greater risk, blurring accountability, and resulting in a disproportionate use of force in violation of international humanitarian law. I thank you, Chair.
I thank the Deputy Permanent Representative of Slovenia for her statement. And I give the floor to the representative of China.

Chair, I thank Greece, France, and the ROK for jointly convening this meeting. I also listened attentively to the three briefers. We need to stay people-centered and ensure that the development and application of technology is consistent with the shared values of all mankind and social ethics and norms. The purposes and principles of the UN Charter must be observed to prevent AI from becoming a tool for seeking hegemony. Second, ensure safety and controllability. We need to ensure that AI remains under human control at all times and constantly improve the explainability and predictability of AI. We need to respect the sovereignty of all countries, abide by local laws, and oppose the use of AI to interfere in the internal affairs, social systems, and social order of other countries. We should effectively safeguard data security, strengthen protection of critical infrastructure, guarantee personal privacy, and promote the development of universally accepted international rules with the participation, wide participation of all parties. The representative of Panama.

Chair, we would like to thank the briefers for their contribution to the discussion. We attach a great deal of importance to the development of advanced technologies which are to serve mankind, and this includes artificial intelligence. We think it's also important to discuss the military AI internationally. However, today, once again, we're being asked to consider the issue of artificial intelligence. a safe, inclusive and trustworthy intelligence in the context of the Security Council mandate. In order to discuss the military aspects of artificial intelligence, there are also other inclusive platforms, first and foremost, a group of governmental experts on the lethal autonomous weapons system working within the framework of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons. Security Council request to use innovations for technical reasons is not needed. But in practice, it turns out that this system of regulation proposed by the initiators of the meeting today is dangerous because it implies, distinction between good AI technologies and bad ones. And this is the crux of the issue. Who is going to determine which kind of use is responsible and which one isn't? But the attempts to make sure that at the level of Security Council, we have the approaches and stances used by individual states using such a process to replace international legal instruments, including through promoting non-inclusive formats and coalitions, will not take us closer to developing common approaches to the AE issues, including its military aspects. I would like to thank the representative of the Russian Federation for her statement.

Thank you very much, Excellencies, colleagues. I'd first of all like to thank the speakers for their briefings and welcome the initiative taken by Greece to organize this AREA formula meeting with which France is associated. Everyone, I think, understands the scale of the revolution introduced by artificial intelligence. AI and its potential to transform our societies, our economies and our institutions. The Security Council must study this matter in greater detail in order to better identify the opportunities and the potential risks as part of its mandate. And I'd like to share with you three messages. First of all, France is mobilized to build international, multi-actor, inclusive and sustainable governance of AI, putting this in the service of the general interest. There is a risk of IA development happening at different speeds throughout the world, limiting its access to the privileged few. collective responsibility is therefore to come up with a shared framework for governance, following the aspiration for an open, inclusive and safe AI that respects human rights and that is accessible to all. This ambition was at the heart of the AI Action Summit that was held in Paris last February, with the participation of more than 100 countries, governments, researchers, business people and representatives of civil society. The work of the summit made it possible for us to have inclusive discussions in order to define concrete solutions to place AI in the service of the general interest, in the interest of development and the sustainability of progress for all. This is the spirit of Current AI, a new global partnership for AI capacity building launched in Paris, aimed to raise a total of $2.5 billion over the next five years. Secondly, AI must respect international law and this must inspire us in our work at the UN. The Global Digital Compact adopted last September enables us to seize upon the opportunities offered by emerging technologies, including AI, whilst addressing the risks related to possible misuse. France calls for the rapid establishment of the independent scientific dialogue on AI governance that is referenced in the Global Digital Compact, and France fully supports Spain and Costa Rica that are co-facilitating this process. This new architecture will make it possible to share information on a common approach to AI. The work of the Security Council will undoubtedly benefit from this. France supports the initiatives and the processes aimed at including development of military AI in terms of respect for international law, particularly international humanitarian law. This is very important, particularly in the area of defence. at the summit in Paris for AI action we adopted a declaration supported by 27 states on maintaining human control over weapons systems involving AI in this declaration we affirmed our commitment to never transfer the decision of life or death to machines operating Beyond any human control and our willingness to continue to participate in multilateral dialogue on these issues France therefore is part of the RE-AIM process in its efforts to understand what is at stake in the military domain with regard to AI. So, colleagues, whilst taking account of these emerging challenges, the Council and the subsidiary bodies must increase their efforts to make better use of the benefits of AI. The AI technologies have potential to provide valuable support, for example, to the monitoring of embargoes or to peacekeeping operations as they implement their mandates. In conclusion, France is prepared to contribute to the work of the Council to make progress for the responsible use of AI for the good of international peace and security. I thank you.

I thank the Permanent Deputy Representative of France for your statement.

I call to the representative of Sierra Leone.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Sierra Leone thanks the delegations of Greece, France, and the Republic of Korea for convening this important AREA Formula meeting, co-sponsored by Armenia, Italy, and the Kingdom of Netherlands. We also extend our appreciation to today's briefers for their insightful contributions. Artificial intelligence holds immense potential to support international peace and security when developed and applied ethically. If harnessed responsibly, AI can assist in addressing some of the root causes and consequences of conflict, including terrorism, food security, climate-related disasters, and fragile governance. AI is also susceptible to misuse. It must be developed and deployed in a manner that fully respects international law, including international human rights and humanitarian law, and is guided by ethical principles that place human dignity, agency, and equity at the center. In particular, We are concerned about the implications of generative AI in spreading disinformation, amplifying hate speech against women and minorities, and enabling cybersecurity attacks and information operations that erode trust in democratic institutions and public order. Improper or malicious uses of AI, including the creation of deep fakes or synthetic media, pose real risks to electoral integrity, freedom of expression, and the right to self-determination under the UN Charter. The use of AI to conduct surveillance or to repress dissent, including by non-state actors and armed groups, can further threaten national and international peace and security. From a security perspective, the development of AI-powered autonomous weapons and robotic systems, if acquired by terrorists or transnational criminal networks, could have destabilizing consequences, especially in fragile regions or conflict-affected states. The absence of human oversight in such systems also raises profound moral and legal questions. At the same time, we recognize the opportunities that AI can provide to strengthen peace efforts. AI can support enhanced decision making, early warning, and predictive analysis for conflict prevention and humanitarian response. It has already been used in some context to monitor ceasefires, detect patterns of violence, and help humanitarian agencies coordinate relief more effectively. AI-driven tools can also aid in combating trafficking and organized crimes. For these reasons, Sierra Leone affirms the African Union's position that artificial intelligence must be governed by frameworks that are open, inclusive, equitable, and trustworthy. The AU's continental artificial intelligence strategy and the African digital compact adopted in 2024 are timely and visionary. They emphasize responsible AI development aligned with regional needs and ethical imperatives. At the AU's Peace and Security Council meeting held on 19th March 2025, African member states reiterated the need for multilateral action to ensure AI promotes peace, security, and sustainable development on the continent. At the national level, Sierra Leone has taken proactive steps. We are party to the Malabo Convention on Cybersecurity and Personal Data Protection and have developed a national cybersecurity strategy that aligns with regional and global digital governance norms. This strategy emphasizes safeguarding digital infrastructure, regulating data access, and ensuring digital technologies do not become tools of exploitation or instability. We are also in the process of developing a national artificial intelligence framework with a focus on ethics, inclusion, and peace-oriented innovation. This framework aims to strengthen national institution capacity to understand, govern, and responsibly deploy AI. With the above said, Mr. Chair, allow me to share four key recommendations. First, in line with the interdisciplinary and multi-stakeholder approach of the Global Digital Compact and the Pact for the Future, we encourage international organizations to deepen engagement with governments, peacebuilders, civil society, academia, and the private sector to co-design AI systems that are tailored to promoting peace, development, and resilience. especially in post-conflict settings. Second, there is a need to establish global norms and principles that hold both states and non-state actors accountable for developing and deploying AI systems with foreseeable risk of undermining peace, fueling conflict, or violating international law. This must include safeguards against militarization of AI as well as accountability for misuse. Third, we are concerned that much of AI development and regulation remains concentrated in a small number of countries and private entities. We call on the United Nations to lead in shaping an inclusive and equitable governance architecture that addresses this imbalance. Measures must be taken to avoid entrenched digital inequality, algorithmic bias, and the concentration of AI capabilities in ways that exclude the global south. The pact for the future rightly emphasizes capacity building, technology transfer and equitable access as prerequisites for shared digital progress. Investing in AI literacy, digital skills and ethical innovation ecosystems in developing countries is essential for preventing asymmetries that could widen geopolitical or digital divides. Fourth, Despite the rapid uptake of AI technologies, there is a clear lack of empirical data on the extent and impact of AI applications in conflict settings. Sierra Leone calls for a comprehensive global mapping and risk assessment of AI use in military and peace and security domains. to inform appropriate regulation, safeguards, and cooperative frameworks. Mr. Chair, Sierra Leone also urges that all AI development be rooted in fundamental principles of transparency, fairness, inclusivity, accountability, and respect for human rights. Those designing the most advanced AI models must be vigilant in addressing algorithmic bias and discriminatory outcomes. Governments, developers, and civil society must work in partnership to ensure that new capabilities are aligned with the UN Charter and the Sustainable Development Goals. There is a fragile line between peace and instability. We believe that digital and emerging technologies, if governed with care, can help countries like ours build resilience and anticipate risk. But if left unregulated or monopolized, these same tools could magnify insecurity, misinformation, and inequality. In conclusion, Mr. Chair, Sierra Leone reaffirms its commitment to working with member states, regional bodies, and the UN system to ensure that artificial intelligence becomes a force for peace and progress, not polarization or conflict. Let us seize this moment to build inclusive global governance for the digital age where innovation supports humanity and technology reinforces the foundations of peace. I thank you.
Thank you, the representative of Sierra Leone for her statement. And now I give the floor to the representative of Somalia.

Breakthrough advances in artificial intelligence we are witnessing offer great opportunity for transformation and development. These opportunities, however, will only be realized if AI is governed in a manner that is truly inclusive and equitable. For Africa, And for the developing world, AI is not merely a technological advancement, but a potential catalyst for leapfrogging development challenges and addressing pressing needs in healthcare, education, agriculture, and governance. The current trajectory of AI development raises important questions about who benefits from these technologies and who shapes the rules that govern. While international initiatives on AI governance are advancing rapidly, we must ensure that these efforts do not widen existing technological and development gaps. Mr. Chair, in conclusion, The potential use of AI to contribute positively to international peace and security is significant. We call on all member states to join us in creating an inclusive approach on AI governance that recognizes the unique perspectives and needs of all nations. Specifically, AI-powered technologies accelerate demining operations by allowing precise mapping of minefields, helping us address one of the greatest humanitarian challenges in the region. Mr. Chair, Azerbaijan remains steadfast in its commitment to harnessing the responsible and ethical advancement of AI, ensuring that the technology aligns with the principles of international peace and security. To that end, we advocate for inclusive governance structures that promote transparency, accountability, and respect for human rights in AI applications. This commitment is essential to prevent the misuse of AI and to safeguard the integrity of our societies. By fostering multilateral dialogue, we can ensure that artificial intelligence contributes to a more peaceful, secure, and prosperous world. Azerbaijan stands ready to actively contribute to this endeavor. Thank you, Mr. Chair.
